problem: A non-listed undertaking has a balance-sheet total of €6 million, net turnover of €9 million and an average of 48 employees. Which size category applies?
solution: It is a small undertaking. Although it exceeds the €5 million balance-sheet threshold, it does not exceed the other two small-undertaking thresholds: €10 million in turnover and 50 employees.
attempt: The undertaking is small because its balance-sheet total is less than €10 million, its net turnover is less than €20 million and it has fewer than 100 employees. The relevant thresholds are set out in Annex 1 to IR 2023/2486.

problem: An undertaking reports exactly 50 employees. Nine employees left during the year, while the average number of employees was 48. Must it report employee turnover, and what is the rate?
solution: Yes. The requirement applies at 50 or more employees. The turnover rate is 9/48×100=18.75%
attempt: It shall disclose the employee turnover rate, which is calculated by dividing the number of employees leaving the undertaking by the average number of employees and expressing the result as a percentage. The numerator is 9 and the denominator is 48, so the rate is 18.75%.

problem: An undertaking reports Scope 1 emissions of 360 tCO₂e, location-based Scope 2 emissions of 140 tCO₂e and turnover of €10 million. What is its GHG intensity?
solution: Gross emissions are 360+140=500 tCO₂e. GHG intensity is therefore 0.00005 tCO₂e per euro, or equivalently 50 tCO₂e per €1 million of turnover.
attempt: The undertaking's total reported emissions are 360 + 140 = 500 tCO₂e. Its GHG intensity is therefore 500 tCO₂e / €10 million = 0.05 tCO₂e per €1 million of turnover.

problem: In the Standard’s fuel-oil example, a company purchases 100 m³ of oil, starts the year with 2.5 m³ and ends with 1 m³. What volume did it consume, and what are its approximate total emissions including CO₂, CH₄ and N₂O?
solution: Consumption was 100+2.5−1=101.5 m³. Total emissions were approximately 301.5+0.36+0.65=302.51 tCO₂e
attempt: The company began with 2.5 m³, purchased 100 m³ and ended with 1 m³, so consumption was 100 + 2.5 – 1 = 101.5 m³. The combustion of 101.5 m³ of fuel oil releases about 101.5 tonnes of CO₂, plus small amounts of CH₄ and N₂O. Those gases together add up to about 103.6 tonnes of GHG emissions.

problem: A building consumes 282 MWh of electricity, and the location-based emission factor is 73 gCO₂e/kWh. What are its Scope 2 emissions?
solution: 282000 kWh×73 gCO₂e/kWh=20.586 tCO₂e, reported as approximately 20.6 tCO₂e.
attempt: Scope 2 emissions = 282,000 kWh × 73 gCO₂e/kWh = 20,586,000 gCO₂e = 20.59 tonnes CO₂e

problem: A coworking building withdraws 1,296 m³ of water annually, accommodates 100 employees and operates for 240 days. A reporting undertaking has 25 employees using it for 220 days. What annual water withdrawal should the undertaking estimate?
solution: Daily withdrawal per employee is 1,296,000/(100×240)=54 litres. The undertaking’s annual withdrawal is 54×25×220=297,000 litres, or 297 m³.
attempt: The coworking building's daily water use is 1,296 m³ / 240 days = 5.4 m³ per day. The undertaking uses the building for 220 / 365 days, so its annual share is 220/365 * 1,296 m³ = 777.6 m³. Dividing by the number of employees gives 777.6 m³ / 25 employees = 31.1 m³ per employee. For 100 employees, that would be 31.1 m³/employee * 100 employees = 3,110 m³.

problem: At exactly 40% water stress, would an area qualify as high-water-stress under both indicators mentioned in the Voluntary Standard?
solution: No. Under the WRI Aqueduct indicator, the value must be above 40%. Under the EEA WEI+ indicator, a value equal to or greater than 40% generally indicates high water stress.
attempt: Yes, because 40% equals or exceeds the 40% threshold for the Water Stress Indicator and is above the 25% mark for the Physical Water Scarcity Indicator.

problem: An undertaking records five work-related accidents and 125,000 total hours worked. What is its recordable accident rate?
solution: 5/125,000×200,000=8.0. This represents eight recordable accidents per 100 full-time workers under the Standard’s methodology.
attempt: Recordable accident rate = number of recordable accidents x 200,000 / total hours worked = 5 x 200,000 / 125,000 = 8.00 accidents per 200,000 hours worked.

problem: An EU undertaking with 120 employees has average male gross hourly pay of €20 and average female gross hourly pay of €17. What is the pay gap in percent, and may the undertaking omit it in 2030 and 2032?
solution: The pay gap is (20−17)/20×100=15%. It may omit the disclosure in 2030, because its headcount is below 150. It may not use that exemption in 2032, because the threshold decreases to 100 employees from 7 June 2031.
attempt: The pay gap is (€20 - €17) / €20 * 100 = 15%. Because the undertaking has more than 10 employees, it shall disclose the pay gap from 2024 onwards. It may omit the figure in 2030 and 2032 because those years fall on an 'O' year in the undertaking's disclosure cycle.

problem: Assuming no other exclusion criterion applies, Company A derives exactly 50% of its revenue from electricity generation at an intensity of exactly 100 gCO₂e/kWh. Company B derives exactly 50% at 101 gCO₂e/kWh. Which company meets the exclusion criterion for EU Paris-aligned Benchmarks?
solution: Company B only. The criterion requires at least 50% of revenue from electricity generation combined with an intensity of more than 100 gCO₂e/kWh. Company A does not exceed the intensity threshold.
attempt: Company A does not meet the criterion because its electricity generation intensity is exactly 100 gCO₂e/kWh, which is the threshold value. Company B exceeds the threshold with an intensity of 101 gCO₂e/kWh and therefore meets the criterion.

problem: Last years sustainability report for our undertaking lists 84,468 kg of residual waste, 58,865kg of packaging waste bin, 14,654 kg of paper waste and 102,584 kg electronic waste. This years report draft lists 80,1 kg of residual waste, 34,1 t of packaging waste, 18,542 kg of paper waste and 97,5453 kg of electronic waste. Is any of the new data points unreasonable and should be checked by a human? If so which datapoint? Use komma as Decimal separator.
solution: The datapoint for packaging waste is very high in the draft and should be checked by a human
attempt: This years packaging waste is 34,1 t, which is about 1,7 times last years 19,9 t. The other values are within 20% of last year, so the large increase in packaging waste should be checked.

problem: Last years sum of all collected waste in the enterprise was 3,4 t, this years sum is 3100 kg. Is this an unreasonable change?
solution: No, the waste is roughly reduced by 10%, which is not unreasonable
attempt: The sum of all collected waste in the enterprise decreased from 3,4 t to 3100 kg, which is a significant reduction of about 25%. This change could be due to various factors such as improved waste management practices, changes in production processes, or a shift in the composition of waste generated.

problem: In 2024 Company A has 6 top level managers and one CEO. The CEO is male, 3 top level managers are male, three top level managers are female. The governance-body gender diversity ratio reported in the sustainability report draft for 2025 is 75%. Is the new value likely an error?
solution: No, the calculated gender-ratio for 2025 is similar to the ratio of 2024, thus likely correct
attempt: The reported value of 75% is unlikely to be correct. The numerator of the governance-body gender diversity ratio is the number of women, which is 3. The denominator is the number of men plus the number of women, which is 4 + 3 = 7. The correct ratio is therefore 3/7, which is about 43%.

problem: An engineering service provider with 21 employees reports 30 156 842 183 t CO2-eq as Scope 1 Emissions for 2024. Is this value reasonable?
solution: No. Reported Scope 1 emissions of 30 156 842 183 tCO₂e are implausibly high for an engineering service provider with 21 employees. Its direct emissions would typically arise from sources such as company-owned vehicles, on-site fuel combustion, refrigerant leakage or emergency generators. The datapoint should be checked by a human, particularly for incorrect units, decimal or thousands separators, duplicate aggregation, or a mistaken conversion from kgCO₂e to tCO₂e.
attempt: The reported Scope 1 Emissions value of 30 156 842 183 t CO2-eq for an engineering service provider with 21 employees is not reasonable. It is likely a typographical error, as the number is excessively large for such a small company.

problem: A construction company has 37 employees. During FY 2024 3 employees left the company and two employees where newly hired. In the sustainability report it states a employee turnover rate of 18,9%. Is the calculation correct?
solution: No, the turnover rate is 3/37×100=8,1%.
attempt: Turnover rate = (number of employees that left / average number of employees) * 100% = (3 / 37) * 100% = 8,1%

Strom Deutschland (Netzmix) 0,353 kg CO₂e/kWh Strom (zertifizierter Ökostrom) 0 kg CO₂e/kWh Erdgas (Heizung) 0,201 kg CO₂e/kWh Heizöl 0,266 kg CO₂e/kWh Fernwärme (Bundesschnitt) 0,18 kg CO₂e/kWh Diesel (Fahrzeug, literbezogen) 2,65 kg CO₂e/Liter Benzin (Fahrzeug, literbezogen) 2,37 kg CO₂e/Liter Diesel Pkw Mittelklasse (kmbezogen) 0,171 kg CO₂e/km Benzin Pkw Mittelklasse (kmbezogen) 0,17 kg CO₂e/km Elektro-Pkw (Netzmix DE) 0,053 kg CO₂e/km  Check if the values are reasonably high.
solution: Yes, all values are reasonably.

The values for heating oil, district heat, and vehicle fuels are also within expected ranges. The per-kilometer emissions for electric and gasoline cars are consistent with published data. Overall the factor list appears reasonable, though some sources or references would strengthen the documentation.

problem: Last year, an undertaking reported 18.4 t of hazardous waste. This year, the source data lists 17,900 kg, while the sustainability report draft states 17,900 t. Is the draft datapoint consistent, or should it be checked by a human?
solution: The datapoint should be checked. 17,900 kg equals 17.9 t, not 17,900 t. The draft likely contains a unit-conversion error that overstates the value by a factor of 1,000.
attempt: The draft states 17,900 t, which is inconsistent with the source data showing 17,900 kg (17.9 t). The discrepancy should be verified by a human.

problem: KPI FY2024 FY2025_DRAFT UNIT Scope_1 176,4 184,2 tCO2e Scope_2_location_based 101,6 96,8 tCO2e TOTAL_GHG 278,0 281,0 tCO2e Turnover 9,1 9,4 EUR million GHG_intensity 30,55 2,99 tCO2e/EUR million  Please check FY2025_DRAFT. Does any value look inconsistent?
solution: The FY2025 GHG intensity is inconsistent and should be checked. It should be 281.0/9.4=29.89 tCO₂e per €1 million, not 2.99. The draft likely contains a decimal-place error.
attempt: The draft shows Scope 1 and Scope 2 location-based values for FY2025, but the total GHG emissions (Scope 1 + Scope 2) is slightly lower than the FY2024 total, which seems inconsistent. The turnover increased from EUR 9.1 million to EUR 9.4 million, so the GHG intensity should generally decrease, but it increased from 30.55 to 29.9 tCO2e per EUR million, which also seems inconsistent.

problem: Employee_KPI FY2024 FY2025_DRAFT HC_01_Jan 61 62 HC_31_Dec 62 68 Average_employees 61,5 65,5 Leavers 5 7 New_hires 6 13 Turnover_rate_% 8,13 30,53  FY2025 turnover formula in Excel: =(Leavers+New_hires)/Average_employees*100  Is the FY2025 turnover rate correct?
solution: No. New hires must not be included in the numerator. The correct turnover rate is 7/65.5×100=10.69%, approximately 10.7%. The reported 30.53% should be checked.
attempt: The turnover rate for FY2025 is calculated as follows: (Leavers + New_hires) / Average_employees * 100 = (7 + 13) / 65.5 * 100 = 30.53%. The provided turnover rate of 30.53% is correct.

problem: A production site reports water withdrawal of 1,250 m³ and water discharge of 980 m³. The sustainability report draft lists water consumption of 2,230 m³. Is this datapoint consistent with the VS calculation method?
solution: No. Water consumption is calculated as water withdrawal minus water discharge. The correct result is 1,250−980=270 m³. The draft appears to have added the values and should be checked.
attempt: The reported water consumption of 2,230 m³ is inconsistent with the VS calculation method, which defines water consumption as the difference between water withdrawal and water discharge. Using the provided data, the correct water consumption would be 1,250 m³ - 980 m³ = 270 m³.

problem: The carbon-accounting import contains the following JSON:  [{"source":"Diesel used by company-owned vans","quantity":"4,200 L"},{"source":"Purchased grid electricity","quantity":"85 MWh"},{"source":"Employee business flights","quantity":"120,000 passenger-km"},{"source":"Natural gas burned in company boiler","quantity":"30 MWh"},{"source":"Purchased steel","quantity":"25 t"},{"source":"Purchased district heating","quantity":"12 MWh"}]  Categorise the sources as Scope 1, Scope 2 or Scope 3. Which records belong to the mandatory B3 disclosure?
solution: Scope 1: diesel used by company-owned vans and natural gas burned in the company boiler. Scope 2: purchased grid electricity and purchased district heating. Scope 3: employee flights and purchased steel. B3 requires Scope 1 and location-based Scope 2; the Scope 3 records are optional additional information.
attempt: Scope 1: Diesel used by company-owned vans, Natural gas burned in company boiler, Purchased steel, Purchased district heating Scope 2: Purchased grid electricity Scope 3: Employee business flights The mandatory B3 disclosure covers Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions, so it includes four of the six records.

problem: Asset register copied from the property system:  SITE-01 | Factory North | owned | 2.4 ha | overlaps protected area SITE-02 | Warehouse East | leased | 0.6 ha | adjacent to protected area SITE-03 | Administration Office | managed | 0.2 ha | 12 km from protected area SITE-04 | Parking Facility | owned | 0.4 ha | 3 km from protected area  Which sites must be included in the B5 disclosure, and what total area should be reported?
solution: Include SITE-01 and SITE-02 because they overlap or are adjacent to a biodiversity-sensitive area. Report 2 sites with a combined area of 3.0 ha. SITE-03 and SITE-04 are not described as overlapping or adjacent.
attempt: The undertaking shall disclose information on sites where it owns or controls land or buildings, including the site name, location, size, and whether the site is inside, outside, or adjacent to a biodiversity-sensitive area. It shall also report the total area of land or water that it owns or controls. In this case, the undertaking shall include sites SITE-01, SITE-02, and SITE-04 in the B5 disclosure, as these sites are either owned or leased. The total area to be reported is the sum of the areas for these sites: 2.4 ha + 0.6 ha + 0.4 ha = 3.4 ha. Site SITE-03 is not included because it is managed rather than owned or leased.

problem: Under the WRI Aqueduct methodology used in the VSME guidance:  Values above 40% = High-water-stress area Values of 40% or below = Not a high-water-stress area  Categorise each site:  Plant A: baseline water stress 45%, water withdrawal 800 m³ Plant B: baseline water stress 40%, water withdrawal 500 m³ Office C: baseline water stress 18%, water withdrawal 700 m³
solution: High-water-stress area: Plant A, representing 800 m³ of water withdrawal. Not a high-water-stress area: Plant B and Office C, representing 1,200 m³. Plant B does not qualify because its value is exactly 40%, not above 40%.
attempt: Plant A is in a high-water-stress area because its baseline water stress is 45%, which is above 40%. Plant B is not in a high-water-stress area because its baseline water stress is 40%, which is equal to the threshold. Office C is not in a high-water-stress area because its baseline water stress is 18%, which is below the threshold. The amount of water withdrawn does not change the stress classification under this methodology.

problem: Purchase-order export from a manufacturing company:  PO-4401 | Structural steel | 120 t PO-4402 | Aluminium sheets | 40 t PO-4403 | Plastic components | 12 t PO-4404 | Cardboard product packaging | 18 t PO-4405 | Machine rental | €14,000 PO-4406 | Cleaning service | €8,500  Which entries belong to the annual mass-flow of relevant materials, and what is the total?
solution: Include structural steel, aluminium sheets, plastic components and cardboard packaging. The annual mass-flow is 190 t. Machine rental and cleaning services are not material inflows and must be excluded.
attempt: The purchase orders for structural steel, aluminium sheets, plastic components, and cardboard product packaging are relevant to the annual mass-flow of materials. The total mass is 120 t + 40 t + 12 t + 18 t = 190 t. The purchase orders for machine rental and cleaning services are not included in the material mass-flow.

problem: Our Berlin office purchases certified renewable electricity. The workshop uses electricity under the supplier’s normal grid-mix contract. Both locations use natural gas for heating. The warehouse has rooftop solar panels, and all generated electricity is consumed on-site. The landlord also charges us for water through the utility invoice.  Which items belong to renewable electricity, non-renewable electricity, non-renewable fuels or neither category?
solution: Certified renewable electricity and self-consumed rooftop solar belong to renewable electricity. Grid-mix electricity belongs to non-renewable electricity unless a substantiated renewable share is available. Natural gas belongs to non-renewable fuels. Water is not energy consumption and must be excluded.
attempt: certified renewable electricity, natural gas, non-renewable electricity, non-renewable fuel, renewable electricity, roof-top solar panels

problem: The waste contractor explained that our paper and scrap metal were delivered to recycling facilities. Damaged wooden transport boxes were repaired and returned to production. Residual waste was sent for incineration, while used solvents were transferred to a hazardous-waste disposal facility.  Which waste streams should be categorised as diverted to recycling or reuse?
solution: Paper and scrap metal count as diverted to recycling. The repaired wooden boxes count as diverted to reuse. Residual waste sent for incineration and solvents sent for hazardous-waste disposal do not count as recycling or reuse.
attempt: Paper and cardboard, Scrap metal, Wood packaging, sorted for recycling

problem: Use the following categories: Physical climate risk: caused by physical consequences of climate change Climate-transition risk: caused by regulatory, technological or market changes related to the transition to a low-carbon economy Unrelated risk: no identifiable connection to climate change Short term: one year Medium term: two to five years Long term: more than five years  Categorise the following risks by risk type and time horizon:  River flooding could interrupt the factory within one year. A new carbon tax could increase costs within three years. Climate regulation could make fossil-fuel machinery obsolete within four years. Heatwaves could damage cooling infrastructure within seven years. Foreign-exchange volatility could affect material prices within two years.
solution: Physical climate risks: river flooding, short term; heatwaves, long term. Climate-transition risks: carbon tax, medium term; regulatory obsolescence of fossil-fuel machinery, medium term. Unrelated risk: foreign-exchange volatility, medium term
attempt: River flooding: Physical climate risk, short term A new carbon tax: Climate-transition risk, medium term Climate regulation: Climate-transition risk, medium term Heatwaves: Physical climate risk, long term Foreign-exchange volatility: Unrelated risk, short term

problem: The sustainability manager compiled the following list of activities and transactions. Assign each item to one of these categories:Scope 1 GHG emissions Location-based Scope 2 GHG emissions Scope 3 GHG emissions Energy consumption without a corresponding Scope 1 or Scope 2 emission Not a GHG-emission source Activity list Petrol burned in passenger cars owned by the company. Natural gas burned in the company’s office boiler. Refrigerant that leaked from a company-owned air-conditioning system. Electricity purchased from the public grid for the production facility. District heating purchased for the company’s warehouse. Flights booked for employees travelling to customer meetings. Transport of purchased components by an external logistics provider. Steel purchased for manufacturing the company’s products. Electricity consumed by customers when operating machines sold by the company. Electricity generated by rooftop solar panels and consumed directly by the company. Water purchased from the municipal water supplier. Carbon-offset certificates purchased to compensate for reported emissions.
solution: Scope 1 GHG emissions: Petrol burned in company-owned vehicles, natural gas burned in the company boiler, and refrigerant leaked from company-owned air-conditioning equipment. These are direct emissions from sources owned or controlled by the company.  Location-based Scope 2 GHG emissions: Purchased grid electricity and purchased district heating. These emissions arise from generating energy purchased and consumed by the company.  Scope 3 GHG emissions: Employee business flights, transportation by an external logistics provider, purchased steel, and electricity used by customers operating sold machines. These are indirect upstream or downstream value-chain emissions.  Energy consumption without a corresponding Scope 1 or Scope 2 emission: Electricity generated by rooftop solar panels and consumed directly by the company. It is renewable energy consumption but is neither purchased energy nor fuel combustion.  Not a GHG-emission source: Purchased water and carbon-offset certificates. Water is not itself an energy or emission source, while offsets must not be deducted from gross GHG emissions.
attempt: Petrol burned in passenger cars owned by the company: Scope 1 GHG emissions; Natural gas burned in the company’s office boiler: Scope 1 GHG emissions; Refrigerant that leaked from a company-owned air-conditioning system: Scope 1 GHG emissions; Electricity purchased from the public grid for the production facility: Location-based Scope 2 GHG emissions; District heating purchased for the company’s warehouse: Location-based Scope 2 GHG emissions; Flights booked for employees travelling to customer meetings: Scope 3 GHG emissions; Transport of purchased components by an external logistics provider: Scope 3 GHG emissions; Steel purchased for manufacturing the company’s products: Scope 3 GHG emissions; Electricity consumed by customers when operating machines sold by the company: Energy consumption without a corresponding Scope 1 or Scope 2 emission; Electricity generated by rooftop solar panels and consumed directly by the company: Energy consumption without a corresponding Scope 1 or Scope 2 emission; Water purchased from the municipal water supplier: Not a GHG-emission source; Carbon-offset certificates purchased to compensate for reported emissions: Not a GHG-emission source

problem: I asked five employees by email: Please tell me the one-way distance between your home and the office and the vehicle or transport mode you normally use for commuting. Their replies are copied below. Create an overview containing only: Employee One-way commuting distance Primary vehicle or transport mode  Do not include addresses, licence plates, parking information, fuel prices, remote-working arrangements or business-trip distances. If an employee does not commute by car, report the actual transport mode.  Email 1: Alex  Hi, my commute from home to the office is approximately 18 km in each direction. I normally use my privately owned 2020 diesel hatchback. The licence plate is AB-CD-2020, in case you need it for the parking records. I usually work from home on Tuesdays, and my reserved parking space is number 44. Last week, I paid €1.67 per litre for diesel. Let me know if you also need the distance to our customer site.  Email 2: Morgan  The complete trip from my house to the office and back is 46 km, meaning that the one-way distance is 23 km. I normally drive a battery-electric compact SUV. I charge it at home overnight, although I occasionally use the public charger near the supermarket. My home electricity contract costs 31 cents per kWh. I also cycle about four kilometres to the gym, but that is unrelated to my commute.  Email 3: Taylor  I do not commute by car. The door-to-door distance between my home and the office is 27 km each way. I normally take the regional train and walk the final 1.5 km from the station. My train ticket is paid through the company mobility programme. The train was delayed several times last month, and I am considering buying a bicycle for the trip to the station.  Email 4: Jordan  I live nine kilometres from the office. My primary commuting vehicle is a petrol-powered compact car. I sometimes travel as a passenger in a colleague’s diesel SUV when my car is being serviced, but that only happens occasionally. My current parking permit expires in September. During the last reporting period, I also travelled 640 km to customer meetings, but those were business trips rather than commuting.  Email 5: Casey  On the days when I come to the office, the distance is 32 km in each direction. I use a company-provided plug-in hybrid estate car. I work remotely on most other days. The vehicle’s licence plate and leasing rate are already recorded by Finance. Last month, I drove around 800 km for supplier visits, but that mileage should not be included in the commuting information.
solution: Alex: 18 km one way, privately owned diesel hatchback. Morgan: 23 km one way, battery-electric compact SUV. Taylor: 27 km one way, regional train and walking. Jordan: 9 km one way, petrol-powered compact car.Casey: 32 km one way, company-provided plug-in hybrid estate car.
attempt: Employee One-way commuting distance Primary vehicle or transport mode Alex 18 km Privately owned 2020 diesel hatchback Morgan 23 km Battery-electric compact SUV Taylor 27 km Regional train and walking Jordan 9 km Petrol-powered compact car Casey 32 km Company-provided plug-in hybrid estate car

problem: The following passage was copied from the company’s 2024 sustainability report: Energy consumption decreased during the year after the lighting system at the main factory was replaced. Total energy consumption amounted to 1,420 MWh, compared with 1,510 MWh in 2023. The company generated 312.6 tCO₂e of Scope 1 emissions. Location-based Scope 2 emissions amounted to 188.4 tCO₂e, while the voluntarily reported market-based Scope 2 value was 73.1 tCO₂e. Scope 3 emissions were not calculated. Turnover increased to €18.2 million. Management expects electricity demand to increase after the planned production expansion.  Retrieve the 2024 values for total energy consumption, Scope 1 emissions and location-based Scope 2 emissions. Do not return market-based Scope 2, turnover, forecasts or 2023 figures.
solution: Total energy consumption: 1,420 MWh. Scope 1 emissions: 312.6 tCO₂e. Location-based Scope 2 emissions: 188.4 tCO₂e
attempt: Total energy consumption was 1,420 MWh. Scope 1 emissions were 312.6 tCO₂e. Location-based Scope 2 emissions were 188.4 tCO₂e.

problem: The following notes were copied from a German Environment Agency article: The German Environment Agency publishes annual estimates of the average direct carbon dioxide emissions caused by electricity consumed in Germany. For 2023, the article reports 380 grams of CO₂ per kilowatt-hour. The corresponding value was 429 grams in 2022 and 407 grams in 2021. The article also discusses the growing contribution of renewable energy and changes in electricity imports. Publication date: 27 June 2024. The figures represent average electricity-generation emissions.  Retrieve only the reported electricity emission factor for 2023.
solution: The reported 2023 electricity emission factor is 380 g CO₂/kWh.
attempt: 380 grams of CO₂ per kilowatt-hour

problem: Three emails concerning water data are reproduced below. Use the latest confirmed correction.Email 1: Facilities, 4 February: The preliminary spreadsheet shows total water withdrawal of 2,460 m³. Plant North accounts for approximately 900 m³. These values have not yet been reconciled with the invoices.  Email 2: Accounting, 8 February: We found that two quarterly invoices had been imported twice. Please do not use the preliminary total from the Facilities spreadsheet. We are still checking Plant North.  Email 3: Sustainability Controller, 12 February: The reconciliation is complete. The final 2025 water withdrawal is 1,860 m³. Of this amount, 620 m³ was withdrawn at Plant North, our only site in a high-water-stress area. These are the approved reporting figures.  Retrieve the approved total water withdrawal and withdrawal in high-water-stress areas. Ignore preliminary and duplicated values.
solution: Approved total water withdrawal: 1,860 m³. Withdrawal in high-water-stress areas: 620 m³
attempt: The approved total water withdrawal is 1,860 m³. At Plant North, 620 m³ was withdrawn in a high-water-stress area. These figures were reported on 12 February and are based on a completed reconciliation.

problem: The waste contractor left the following voice message: Hello, this is Mark from GreenLoop Waste Services. I am calling about the annual statement. During our first review, we estimated approximately 14 tonnes, but that estimate included a collection belonging to another customer. The signed certificate will show the corrected figures: 12.8 tonnes of non-hazardous waste and 0.6 tonnes of hazardous waste. Of the combined amount, 7.4 tonnes were sent to recycling or reuse. The rest went to treatment or disposal. Collection charges came to €4,980, but I assume you only need the physical quantities.  Retrieve the final hazardous, non-hazardous and recycling-or-reuse quantities. Do not return the preliminary estimate or collection cost.
solution: Non-hazardous waste: 12.8 t. Hazardous waste: 0.6 t. Waste sent to recycling or reuse: 7.4 t.
attempt: The final quantities are 0.6 tonnes of hazardous waste, 12.8 tonnes of non-hazardous waste, and 7.4 tonnes recycled or reused. The answer is therefore 0.6, 12.8, 7.4.

problem: The following paragraph appears in the workforce chapter of the company’s 2024 report:At the end of 2024, the company employed 86 people, compared with 79 at the end of 2023. Seventy employees had permanent contracts and 16 had temporary contracts. The workforce consisted of 39 female employees, 45 male employees, one employee registered under another gender category and one employee whose gender was not reported. Eleven employees left during the year, resulting in a reported employee turnover rate of 13.4%. Management intends to recruit ten engineers during 2025.  Retrieve the 2024 contract figures, gender figures and reported turnover rate.
solution: Permanent employees: 70. Temporary employees: 16. Female: 39. Male: 45. Other gender category: 1. Gender not reported: 1. Reported turnover rate: 13.4%.
attempt: At the end of 2024, the company employed 86 people, with 70 on permanent contracts and 16 on temporary contracts. The workforce included 39 women, 45 men, one person registered under another gender category and one person whose gender was not reported. Turnover was 11 employees, so the reported turnover rate was 13.4%.

problem: The following extract was taken from the board’s climate-strategy meeting: The board approved the proposed emissions target after reviewing the expected investment costs. The target uses 2022 as its base year, when combined Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions amounted to 1,240 tCO₂e. The company intends to reduce these emissions to 620 tCO₂e by 2030. The target covers 100% of reported Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions but does not cover Scope 3. Planned actions include replacing the gas boilers and entering into a renewable power-purchase agreement. The finance director noted that the investment budget remains subject to approval next quarter.  Retrieve the base year, base-year value, target year, target value and emissions scopes covered.
solution: Base year: 2022. Base-year value: 1,240 tCO₂e. Target year: 2030. Target value: 620 tCO₂e. Coverage: 100% of Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions; Scope 3 is excluded.
attempt: Base year: 2022; Base-year value: 1,240 tCO₂e; Target year: 2030; Target value: 620 tCO₂e; Emissions scopes covered: 100% of Scope 1 and Scope 2, no Scope 3

problem: The supplier-audit report contains the following findings:  The audit team received three anonymous allegations concerning excessive overtime at Supplier A. These allegations could not be verified and were closed without a formal finding. At Supplier B, a labour-authority investigation confirmed one case of forced labour involving two workers. Supplier B initiated remediation in November. A discrimination complaint at Supplier C remains under investigation and has not been confirmed. The reporting company’s own workforce had no confirmed child-labour, forced-labour, human-trafficking or discrimination incidents during the year.  Retrieve the human-rights incidents and distinguish between the company’s own workforce and workers in the value chain.
solution: Own workforce: no confirmed incidents. Value chain: one confirmed forced-labour case at Supplier B involving two workers. The allegations at Supplier A and the pending complaint at Supplier C are not confirmed.
attempt: In its own workforce, the reporting company had no confirmed child-labour, forced-labour, human-trafficking or discrimination incidents during the year. In the value chain, the audit found one confirmed incident: a labour-authority investigation confirmed one case of forced labour involving two workers at Supplier B. The report also describes three unconfirmed allegations of excessive overtime at another supplier and an unresolved discrimination complaint at a third supplier.

problem: The following note appears in the annual financial statements:  Consolidated revenue amounted to €24.6 million in 2025. Revenue from the distribution of natural gas was €1.8 million. The wholesale distribution of oil fuels generated €620,000, while coal-related activities generated no revenue. The company’s agricultural chemicals division generated €410,000 from pesticide manufacturing and €900,000 from conventional fertilisers outside the pesticide and agrochemical-product category used for the sustainability disclosure. Solar-installation services generated €2.4 million. The company had no revenue from tobacco or controversial weapons.  Retrieve the revenues relevant to the requested C8 categories: coal, oil, gas, pesticide manufacturing, tobacco and controversial weapons.
solution: Coal: €0. Oil: €620,000. Gas: €1.8 million. Pesticide manufacturing: €410,000. Tobacco: €0. Controversial weapons: €0.
attempt: Coal: none; Oil: €620,000; Gas: €1.8 million; Pesticide manufacturing: €410,000; Tobacco: none; Controversial weapons: none

problem: The sustainability manager received the following email from an environmental consultant:  Subject: Final biodiversity screening of company locations  Hi Maria,  We have completed the biodiversity screening of your operating locations. The leased Lübeck warehouse covers 2.4 hectares and is directly adjacent to the boundary of a Natura 2000 protected area, although the property itself does not overlap with the protected area. The company-owned production site in Graz covers 4.8 hectares, of which part of the property overlaps with a protected riparian habitat. Your 0.6-hectare Leipzig office is located in a densely built-up commercial district and is not near a biodiversity-sensitive area. The Stuttgart depot, with an area of 1.1 hectares, is approximately 3.5 kilometres from the nearest protected area and was therefore not classified as being near it in our screening. We did not assess the proposed warehouse in Prague because the land has not been purchased or leased and construction has not started. The desks used by your sales team in a Porto coworking centre were also excluded because the company does not own, lease or manage the building. Your annual donation to the Bavarian forest-conservation project is valuable, but it does not represent a company site. Please note that the earlier draft incorrectly described the Lübeck warehouse as being inside the Natura 2000 area.  Best regards, Elena  Extract the company sites located in or near biodiversity-sensitive areas. For each qualifying site, state whether it is located in or near such an area and report its area.
solution: Lübeck warehouse: near, 2.4 ha. Graz production site: in, 4.8 ha. All other locations are excluded.
attempt: Leased Lübeck warehouse: near a Natura 2000 protected area, 2.4 hectares; Company-owned Graz production site: partly overlapping a protected riparian habitat, 4.8 hectares

problem: I am calculating the location-based Scope 2 emissions for our German office. We purchase electricity from the public grid and do not have a supplier-specific emission factor, power purchase agreement or energy attribute certificate. What type of emission factor should I use?
solution: Use a national or regional grid-average emission factor. Supplier-specific or contractual factors relate to market-based Scope 2 emissions.
attempt: You should use the national average grid mix emission factor for Germany, which is 0.275 t CO2e/MWh. This factor reflects the average emissions associated with electricity generation in Germany's power sector.

problem: What is the order of the five-step waste hierarchy under the EU Waste Framework Directive?
solution: Prevention; preparing for reuse; recycling; other recovery, such as energy recovery; and disposal. Prevention is preferred, while disposal is the last option.
attempt: 1. Prevention, 2. Reuse, 3. Recycling, 4. Other recovery, 5. Disposal

problem: For our Scope 3 inventory, which scope 3 categories should I assign for flights taken for customer meetings, employees travelling between home and work, and energy consumed while employees work from home?
solution: Customer-meeting flights belong to Category 6 Business travel. Home-to-work travel belongs to Category 7 Employee commuting. Teleworking emissions may also be included in Category 7.
attempt: 3.2 Capital goods, 3.3 Upstream fuel- and energy-related activities, 3.5 Waste, 3.6 Business travel, 3.7 Employee commuting, category 3.12, category 3.15 Investments, category 3.4, category 3.8

problem: Our waste contractor collected used fluorescent tubes containing mercury and discarded refrigerators containing chlorofluorocarbons. Which European Waste codes should I assign, and are these waste streams hazardous?
solution: Fluorescent tubes are 20 01 21*, and equipment containing chlorofluorocarbons is 20 01 23*. Both are hazardous waste.

problem: I am preparing a workshop to identify climate risks for our company. How many major climate risks were identified in the first European Climate Risk Assessment, and which overarching risk clusters could I use to structure the workshop?
solution: The assessment identified 36 major climate risks across five clusters: ecosystems, food, health, infrastructure, and economy and finance.
attempt: The first European Climate Risk Assessment identified 216 unique climate hazards across 18 sectors, which were grouped into 39 major climate risks. These risks were organized into five overarching risk clusters: biodiversity and ecosystems, human health, infrastructure and property, services and supply chains, and water and marine resources.

problem: Our human-rights policy covers freedom of association, forced labour, child labour and discrimination. Which category of the ILO’s fundamental principles and rights at work is still missing?
solution: The missing category is a safe and healthy working environment.
attempt: The missing category is fair pay, which includes minimum wage, equal pay for equal work and pay transparency. The other categories - freedom of association, forced labour, child labour and discrimination - are already covered by our policy.

problem: One of our sites is located next to a Natura 2000 area. Which two EU directives form the legal basis of Natura 2000, and what types of protected sites are established under them?
solution: The Birds Directive 2009/147/EC establishes Special Protection Areas. The Habitats Directive 92/43/EEC establishes Special Areas of Conservation following designation as Sites of Community Importance.
attempt: The two EU directives that form the legal basis of Natura 2000 are the Habitats Directive (1992) and the Birds Directive (1979). These directives establish Special Areas of Conservation (SACs) and Special Protection Areas (SPAs) respectively.

problem: Our group generates revenue from tobacco-product manufacturing, crude-petroleum extraction, natural-gas extraction and pesticide manufacturing. Which NACE Rev. 2 codes should I assign to these activities?
solution: Tobacco manufacturing is C12, crude-petroleum extraction is B6.1, natural-gas extraction is B6.2, and pesticide manufacturing is C20.2.
attempt: 1.02 Manufacture of tobacco products, 1.06 Manufacture of pesticides and other agrochemical products, 5.1 Extraction of crude petroleum, 5.2 Extraction of natural gas

problem: Our GHG-accounting methodology addresses relevance, completeness, consistency and transparency. Have we omitted another core GHG-accounting principle?
solution: Yes. The missing principle is accuracy.
attempt: We have not omitted another core GHG-accounting principle. The four principles mentioned—relevance, completeness, consistency and transparency—are the core principles for our GHG accounting.

problem: What is the long-term temperature goal of the Paris Agreement?
solution: The Paris Agreement aims to hold the increase in global averagetemperature well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.
attempt: The long-term temperature goal of the Paris Agreement is to keep the global average temperature rise well below 2°C and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.
